slides.title: [1] Imports, the basin helper, and the bounds
slides.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.optimize import minimize

def basin(x: float, y: float, cx: float,
          cy: float, depth: float,
          wx: float, wy: float) -> float:
    """One Gaussian dip at (cx, cy), 'depth' deep."""
    return -depth * np.exp(-(((x-cx)**2)/(2*wx**2)
                             + ((y-cy)**2)/(2*wy**2)))

BOUNDS = [(0.20, 0.60), (0.0, 1.2)]
slides.explainHead: Every line, exactly as Week 9 had it
slides.explainBody: Nothing is abbreviated here. basin() returns one NEGATIVE Gaussian dip — deepest at (cx, cy), fading toward zero far away — and it carries the one-line docstring plus parameter and return type hints this course has required since Week 4. BOUNDS is the same (min, max)-per-variable list Week 10's linprog used. The next cell adds the two dips together into energy_proxy and checks the result against Week 9's numbers.
slides.teaching: Read basin()'s signature out loud — seven floats in, one float out. Point at the docstring and remind students this is the same convention their own functions have needed since Week 4; it is not decoration.

slides.title: [1] continued: energy_proxy, then the continuity check
slides.code:
def energy_proxy(v: tuple) -> float:
    """Energy-use proxy at one (wwr, shade_m) pair."""
    w, s = v
    base = 20.0
    b1 = basin(w, s, 0.52, 0.25, 30.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    b2 = basin(w, s, 0.28, 0.90, 34.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    ridge = 6.0 * np.exp(-((w-0.40)**2)/0.02)
    return base + b1 + b2 + ridge

print('local:', round(energy_proxy((0.52, 0.25)), 2))
print('lower:', round(energy_proxy((0.28, 0.90)), 2))
slides.explainHead: A continuity check, not a fresh scenario
slides.explainBody: energy_proxy adds a shallower and a deeper basin to a flat base, plus a ridge that separates them. If the printed values are not -7.08 and -11.08, fix the copied function before continuing. 'Lower' is descriptive; the global claim still needs proof beyond this finite evidence.
slides.teaching: Confirm the Week 9 values, then say explicitly: lower/best known is not the same as proved global.

slides.title: Studio 1: predict before you run Demo A
slides.prompt: A starting guess of wwr=0.55, shade=0.20 looks like a reasonable design to try.
steps: State your prediction: which basin (local or global) will this land in?
Name what you are using to make that prediction.
Run cell [2] and compare.
Note whether result.success being True changed your confidence -- it should not have.
slides.teaching: Most students will not confidently predict LOCAL here — that uncertainty is expected and is the point.

slides.title: [2] DEMO A — a plausible starting guess
slides.code:
result_a = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.55, 0.20),
                    bounds=BOUNDS)
print('x:', result_a.x.round(4))
print('value:', round(result_a.fun, 4))
print('success:', result_a.success)
slides.explainBody: success is True. Nothing here signals a problem. This is exactly the reported result Project 2 would grade as final if only one starting guess were ever tried.
slides.teaching: Pause here before showing Demo B — ask students to commit to a written prediction of what will change.

slides.title: [3] DEMO B — only x0 changes
slides.code:
result_b = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.20, 1.00),
                    bounds=BOUNDS)
print('x:', result_b.x.round(4))
print('value:', round(result_b.fun, 4))
print('success:', result_b.success)

print('improvement over Demo A:',
      round(result_b.fun - result_a.fun, 2))
slides.output:
x: [0.2763 0.9   ]
value: -11.1437
success: True
improvement over Demo A: -3.99
slides.explainBody: Roughly a 4-point improvement — a real, material difference in this energy proxy, produced by changing nothing except where the search started.
slides.teaching: Ask: if a student had only run Demo A and submitted it, what would be lost? Answer: about 4 points of achievable performance, silently.

slides.title: Recall: result.success does not mean 'best'
slides.definition: A True/False flag meaning the search converged — it stopped because it satisfied its own stopping rule. It does not mean the result is the best point anywhere in bounds.

example.head: Demo A and Demo B, side by side
example.body: Both report success: True. Demo A stopped at -7.1521 (local); Demo B stopped at -11.1437 (lower, best known). Convergence, quality, and proof of globality are three different questions.

slides.note: Reading success alone is exactly the mistake cell [6]'s AI-audit makes next.
slides.teaching: Ask whether a defective single-start function could still print success: True. It can. Then distinguish a lower corroborated result from a proved global optimum.

slides.title: Studio 2: which optimum is actually better, and by how much?
slides.prompt: Two clean, successful minimize results, two different answers.
steps: State which of result_a.fun and result_b.fun is lower (better, since this proxy is minimized).
Compute the improvement Demo B offers over Demo A.
Name the one thing that differed between the two calls.
State in one sentence why 'it converged' is not the same as 'it found the best design.'
slides.teaching: Expected: result_b is lower by about 3.99; only x0 differed; convergence means the search stopped moving, not that it found the true minimum.

slides.title: Same function, same bounds, different answer

left.head: What just happened
left.body: Two calls to minimize(), identical objective, identical bounds — the only difference was the starting guess. That single difference produced two different, both fully 'successful,' results.

right.head: Why this is not a bug
right.body: This is what gradient-based search always risks on a genuinely nonlinear objective with more than one basin. The fix is not a better algorithm — it is never trusting a single run.

slides.teaching: Connect directly to Project 2 Part II's requirement: at least two initial guesses, with the comparison reported, not hidden.

slides.title: [4] Multi-start sweep: one dict per starting guess
slides.code:
starting_guesses = [
    (0.55, 0.20), (0.50, 0.30), (0.40, 0.55),
    (0.45, 0.60), (0.60, 0.10), (0.20, 1.00),
    (0.30, 0.85), (0.22, 1.15),
]
records = []
for wwr0, shade0 in starting_guesses:
    res = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(wwr0, shade0),
                   bounds=BOUNDS)
    records.append({'start_wwr': wwr0,
                    'start_shade': shade0,
                    'final_wwr': round(res.x[0], 4),
                    'final_shade': round(res.x[1], 4),
                    'value': round(res.fun, 4)})
slides.explainHead: New pattern: build a list of one dict per row
slides.explainBody: The eight starting guesses are the verified ones from Meeting A's table. The for-loop is Week 3's pattern, and minimize is called ONCE per pass with that pass's own (wwr0, shade0). What is new is the shape of what gets collected: each pass builds one dict with all five keys — start_wwr, start_shade, final_wwr, final_shade, value — and appends it to records. Nothing is abbreviated; all five keys are written out. After eight passes, records holds eight dicts.
slides.teaching: Point at the indentation: minimize and records.append are both INSIDE the loop, so they run eight times. Ask what records contains right after the loop ends — eight dicts, not a table yet.

slides.title: [4] continued: a list of dicts becomes one table
slides.explainHead: One line turns eight dicts into eight rows
slides.explainBody: pd.DataFrame(records) reads the eight dicts' shared keys as column names and each dict as one ROW — a different shape from Week 4, which always built a DataFrame from one dict of whole COLUMNS. Same function, opposite input shape: know which one you are building. The printed result is exactly Meeting A's eight-row table, now produced by your own loop instead of read off a slide.
slides.teaching: Name this explicitly as new syntax, not a recall — Week 4 only ever built a DataFrame from a dict-of-lists. Have students compare this printout line by line against Meeting A's table before moving on.

parts.body: Same alias as Week 4 — import pandas as pd.

parts.label: Builds a table

parts.label: A list of dicts, one per row

slides.teaching: Point back at cell [4]'s for-loop while showing this — 'records' is the exact list built one dict at a time, right before this line runs.

slides.title: Bonus: sort the sweep by value
slides.explainBody: sort_values('value') reorders the SAME DataFrame from cell [4] by the value column, ascending by default — most negative (best, since this proxy is minimized) first. .head(3) then keeps only the top three. No new numbers here, only a new way to read a table you already built.
slides.teaching: Not a required handout cell — a console-only trick worth showing live. Point out the row labels (6, 7, 5) are the ORIGINAL index positions from cell [4], not renumbered — confirms nothing was recomputed, only re-read.

slides.title: Studio 3: count the split before pandas counts it for you
slides.prompt: Eight rows, two distinct final values, by inspection.
steps: Scan the value column: how many rows show -7.1521? How many show -11.1437?
Write your count down before running cell [5].
Run cell [5] and confirm value_counts() matches your hand count.
State the percentage that landed in the worse (local) optimum.
slides.teaching: Expected: 5 rows at -7.1521, 3 rows at -11.1437, 62.5% local.

slides.title: np.where, defined
slides.definition: np.where(condition, if_true, if_false) — a vectorized if/else — for every row at once, it writes one value where the condition is True and another where it is False, producing a whole new column with no explicit loop.

example.head: np.where(multi_start['value'] < -9, 'LOWER', 'LOCAL')
example.body: Reads every row's value column at once. -9 sits between -7.1521 and -11.1437 — a labeling convenience for these two observed basins, not a global-optimality certificate.

slides.note: Plain Python if/else tests ONE value. np.where tests an entire column and returns an entire column — that is the whole reason it exists.
slides.teaching: Make the vectorized labeling visible before the table, and clarify that LOWER means the lower observed basin rather than a proof label.

slides.title: [5] Classified and counted: 5 of 8 land in the trap
slides.callout: value_counts() on the basin column: LOCAL 5, LOWER 3. LOWER is the best-corroborated basin, not a proof label.
slides.teaching: np.where(multi_start['value'] < -9, 'LOWER', 'LOCAL') uses -9 only to separate these two observed values; it is not a general rule or proof of globality.

slides.title: The 5-3 split, seen as a bar
slides.explainHead: Five out of eight, at a glance
slides.explainBody: Same counts as cell [5]. The taller bar is the worse objective value, so frequency does not establish quality. The LOWER label records relative evidence, not proof of a continuous global optimum.
slides.teaching: Ask which bar looks 'better' if height alone were shown. Height tracks frequency, not quality or proof.

slides.title: Why the starting guess changes the answer

left.head: What minimize can see
left.body: Only the slope at its current position, one step at a time. If that slope points toward the shallower basin, it stops there — with no way to know a deeper basin exists elsewhere.

right.head: The practical rule this buys you
right.body: Never trust a single minimize() call on a nonlinear objective. Run at least two well-separated starting guesses, and report whether they agree — exactly Project 2 Part II's requirement.

slides.teaching: This is the sentence students should be able to say from memory before Wednesday ends.

slides.title: Predict before you run: cell [6]
slides.code:
def ai_find_best_design():
    result = minimize(energy_proxy,
                       x0=(0.55, 0.20))
    print('Minimum energy proxy:',
          round(result.fun, 4))
    return result.x
slides.question: What value will this print?
options: An error, because bounds= is missing
slides.why: x0=(0.55, 0.20) is Demo A's exact start, and this basin sits inside the box anyway, so it prints -7.1521 again. Only the LABEL changed.
slides.teaching: Do not let 'no bounds=' bait students into predicting an error or a wild number — the honest, uncomfortable answer is that it runs cleanly and reproduces Demo A exactly.

slides.title: [6] AI-audit: a single-start optimizer, mislabeled
slides.code:
def ai_find_best_design():
    result = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.55, 0.20))
    print(f'Best design: wwr={result.x[0]:.4f}, shade={result.x[1]:.4f}')
    print(f'Minimum energy proxy: {result.fun:.4f}')
    return result.x

best = ai_find_best_design()
slides.output:
Best design: wwr=0.5241, shade=0.2500
Minimum energy proxy: -7.1521
slides.explainBody: No error, no warning — and a print statement that calls a local result 'Best design' and 'Minimum energy proxy.' Also missing: bounds=, and any check of result.success. Four real, distinct defects in six lines.
slides.teaching: Give students this exact function and this exact output. Require them to name at least four defects before revealing the instructor list.

slides.title: Studio 4: diagnose at least four defects
slides.prompt: This function runs without any error message.
steps: Name the single-start defect and why the print label overreaches.
Name the missing bounds= defect and what it risks in general.
Name the missing result.success check.
Rewrite the function so its label matches what it actually found.
slides.teaching: Require students to reference cells [2]-[5]'s own numbers when naming the mislabeling defect — 'it says Best design but cell [4] shows 5 of 8 starts land here' is the expected level of specificity.

slides.title: [7] Self-check: two new starting guesses, not used above
slides.code:
t1 = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.35, 0.75),
              bounds=BOUNDS)
t2 = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.58, 0.15),
              bounds=BOUNDS)
print('t1:', t1.x.round(4), round(t1.fun, 4))
print('t2:', t2.x.round(4), round(t2.fun, 4))
assert abs(t1.fun - (-11.1437)) < 0.01
assert abs(t2.fun - (-7.1521)) < 0.01
assert t1.fun < t2.fun
slides.explainHead: Neither start appears in cell [4]'s table
slides.explainBody: The new starts reproduce the lower-versus-local basin pattern, so it is not an artifact of the original eight starts. This transfer check corroborates the pattern; it still does not prove -11.1437 is globally minimal over every point.
slides.teaching: This is the required transfer safeguard: different inputs and passing assertions. State the boundary between corroboration and proof.

slides.title: Studio 5: confirm your predictions with asserts
slides.prompt: Before running cell [7], predict which basin each new start reaches.
steps: Predict (0.35, 0.75): closer to the lower basin center (0.28, 0.90) -- which basin?
Predict (0.58, 0.15): closer to the local basin center (0.52, 0.25) -- which basin?
Run cell [7] and confirm both assert statements pass.
Write why this corroborates the two-basin pattern without proving global optimality.
slides.teaching: Expected: (0.35, 0.75) -> LOWER, (0.58, 0.15) -> LOCAL. Proximity predicts these two cases; the transfer check supports the pattern but is not a proof over the continuum.

slides.title: Multi-start, defined
slides.definition: Running the identical objective and bounds from several different, well-separated starting guesses, then comparing every result before reporting any one of them as final.

example.head: Today's script, at two scales
example.body: Two guesses by hand (Demo A and Demo B), then eight in a loop (cell [4]) — both are the same method, multi-start, just at different scale.

slides.teaching: Name this explicitly as the word for what the whole studio has been doing since Demo A — students have been practicing multi-start for the last ten minutes without the label.

slides.title: Solver card, defined
slides.definition: A one-page record of HOW an optimization was run — not just its final answer: algorithm family, every starting guess tried, whether each run converged, and whether multiple runs agreed.

example.head: Required twice in Project 2 Part II
example.body: One solver card for your linprog solution, one for your minimize solution — the next slide lists exactly what belongs in each.

slides.teaching: Preview that this term was named but not yet defined at the end of Meeting A — this is that promised definition.

slides.title: What belongs on a one-page solver card
rows: gradient-based (scipy.optimize.minimize), and why it fits a smooth nonlinear objective
at least two, well-separated, both stated with their results
result.success for each run, plus number of iterations
did the runs agree? if not, which optimum is reported as final, and why
slides.callout: Every optimization in Project 2 needs one of these — for the linprog solution AND the minimize solution.
slides.teaching: Name this as new vocabulary for the first time — Project 2 Part II requires exactly this artifact for both the linprog and the minimize components.

slides.title: Multiple starts expose initialization sensitivity
takeaways: The same function and bounds can report two different, both 'successful,' local optima—only the starting guess changed.
5 of 8 plausible starts land in the worse local optimum (-7.1521); 3 reach the lower best-known basin (-11.1437).
Dense-grid plus multistart agreement corroborates the lower basin; it does not prove a continuous global optimum.
Project 2 Part II requires at least two initial guesses, explicit bounds, solver checks, and honest comparison.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: name two well-separated Project 2 starts, predict agreement, and state what evidence would still be needed before claiming global optimality.
